title: Self-Evolutionary Reinforced Knowledge Distillation for Multi-Modal Tool-Use Agents

problem.claim: Deploying multi-modal large language models for tool use is constrained by computational cost and inference latency.

gap.claim: Small multi-modal agents struggle with limited reasoning capacity, sparse and brittle reward signals, and failure to transfer procedural knowledge through naive distillation.

contributions.claim: A two-stage self-evolutionary knowledge distillation framework equips small multi-modal language models with adaptive tool-use behaviors.
The framework combines mutual information-guided trajectory distillation with reinforcement-driven policy evolution and iterative teacher feedback.

The framework uses weighted semantic objectives, error-driven optimization, hybrid experience replay, and group-relative policy refinement with rewards for answer correctness, invocation validity, and tool effectiveness.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Integrated with interactive tool modules, the approach enables small models to achieve strong performance across diverse tool-use benchmarks.
The authors report consistent improvements over single-pass distillation and reinforcement-learning baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: Multi-modal agents are important for reasoning about complex environments and orchestrating tool use.
The computational cost and latency of large models motivate compact models that retain agentic capabilities.
Small-agent training is hindered by limited capacity, unreliable rewards, and weak procedural transfer from naive distillation.
The proposed framework combines selective trajectory distillation, reinforcement-driven policy evolution, teacher feedback, and stabilizing optimization mechanisms.
The authors report strong benchmark performance and improvements over specified baselines, positioning the framework as a practical deployment path.

source_observation.claim: The method selectively distills high-utility trajectory segments and combines distillation with iterative policy evolution.

interpretation.claim: Selective transfer and feedback-driven refinement may better preserve procedural tool-use behavior than one-pass imitation.

application.claim: For compact tool-use agents, prioritize informative interaction segments and iterative refinement over indiscriminate single-pass distillation.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this strategy generalizes beyond the reported multi-modal tool-use setting.

source_observation.claim: The reward design covers answer correctness, invocation validity, and tool effectiveness.

interpretation.claim: Evaluating multiple dimensions of tool use may address weaknesses caused by sparse or brittle single-purpose rewards.

application.claim: When training tool-use agents, align rewards with both final answers and intermediate invocation quality.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the relative weighting, implementation, or effect of each reward dimension.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the benchmark datasets, model architectures, or experimental configurations.
No quantitative results, metric values, or statistical comparisons are provided.
The abstract does not describe limitations, compute requirements, or failure cases.
